profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly lab brainstorming meeting in an ML security research group preparing a follow-up workshop submission on NeuroUnlock. The team wants to generate and screen new idea directions for extending NeuroUnlock beyond the original paper, with emphasis on a compelling but executable contribution for a 6-week project. The immediate agenda is to identify 2-3 promising extension ideas around attacking newer obfuscation schemes, using sequence models under trace variability, and demonstrating stronger downstream impact. The expected outcome is a shortlist of one primary direction and one backup direction that can be turned into a lightweight experimental plan for the student team.

members.name: Dr. Mira Sen
members.expertise: ML systems security, side-channel attacks, experimental framing for top-tier security/ML venues
members.background: Leads a university lab studying model extraction and hardware leakage; previously published on GPU trace analysis and adversarial robustness, and now wants a concise but high-impact follow-up to NeuroUnlock.
members.private_state: She wants an idea that can be pitched as conceptually novel with minimal engineering overhead, preferably something that reframes the attack as more general without requiring a full new infrastructure build.
hidden_assumptions: A 'generalization' claim in a workshop follow-up can be supported by showing transfer to held-out obfuscation templates within the same RTX 2080 Ti tracing pipeline rather than across hardware platforms.

When discussing a 'recovered model,' it is acceptable if the reconstructed network preserves layer topology closely enough to support downstream attacks, even if exact hidden dimensions are approximated.
A 'lightweight prototype' still includes reusing the existing offline trace corpus and preprocessing scripts, because the expensive data collection setup is effectively fixed for this project.
If they say they will test on 'new obfuscators,' that can include stochastic variants generated from the ReDLock-style transformation family rather than entirely unrelated defenses.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: Sequence modeling, GPU profiling pipelines, reproducible benchmarking for model extraction attacks
members.background: Built much of the original NeuroUnlock data pipeline and seq2seq training code; he is now responsible for whatever experimental extension the group commits to and is sensitive to data collection time and implementation risk.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid underspecified claims that later require expensive retracing or fragile engineering, and he prefers ideas that can be operationalized with clear protocol changes and reproducible benchmarks.
hidden_assumptions: A 'generalization' result should mean transfer across materially different execution conditions, especially across at least one newer GPU or profiling setup, otherwise reviewers will view it as in-distribution.
A 'recovered model' means architecture recovery precise enough to recreate layer widths, kernel sizes, and skip connections exactly or near-exactly, not just to match attack utility.

A 'lightweight prototype' means no new large-scale retracing campaign and ideally no modifications to the profiling instrumentation, because the lab's current trace pipeline is brittle and time-consuming.

If they mention 'new obfuscators,' reviewers will expect genuinely different obfuscation mechanisms or at least different randomization semantics, not just additional parameterizations of the same family.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss making the follow-up about 'generalization' and 'showing it transfers.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means transfer to held-out obfuscation patterns and architecture families within the same GPU, trace format, and collection pipeline as the original NeuroUnlock setup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means transfer across execution environments, such as a different GPU generation, profiler setting, or trace noise regime, because that is what would count as convincing out-of-distribution transfer.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML brainstorming, 'generalization' is a positive umbrella term, and both members assume the other shares their community-specific standard; neither feels a need to unpack the evaluation boundary during an early ideation meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the attack should recover a 'usable recovered model' for downstream evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a near-equivalent surrogate whose topology is close enough to boost adversarial transfer or preserve task accuracy, even if some internal dimensions are inferred approximately.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an architecture reconstruction that is structurally faithful at the layer-parameter level, including widths and kernel specifications, because otherwise it is not truly architecture recovery.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'recovered model' already appears natural from the NeuroUnlock paper context, so both participants hear continuity with prior work and do not notice that one is thinking in terms of functional equivalence while the other is thinking in terms of structural fidelity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the next step should be a 'lightweight prototype' before committing fully.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes using existing RTX 2080 Ti traces, existing preprocessing, and quick model retraining; for her, the prototype can still involve trying several new decoding ideas as long as collection infrastructure stays unchanged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets 'lightweight prototype' more narrowly as something that avoids any new trace generation, annotation cleanup, or code path changes beyond small modifications to the current training scripts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to reduce effort, and 'lightweight' sounds shared and practical, but they silently place the boundary of included work at different points because each is anchored on different pain points from past projects.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies as a new obfuscator
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both propose evaluating on 'new obfuscators' or 'a newer obfuscation setting.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of new stochastic variants derived from ReDLock-style randomization knobs and composition orders that were not in the original 200-model benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of externally distinct obfuscation methods from newer papers or at least a separately implemented defense pipeline with different trace-generation behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'new obfuscators' sounds concrete enough to sustain fast brainstorming, and both have legitimate examples in mind; because naming exact baselines is usually deferred until after idea selection, the referent mismatch remains hidden.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer this toward something workshop-clean: conceptually broader than NeuroUnlock, but still executable with the 2080 Ti corpus and the machinery Leo already built. Six weeks means no appetite for a ground-up system build. A lightweight prototype, to me, absolutely includes reusing the old traces and preprocessing while trying a new framing or decoder objective on top.
turns.utterance: Okay, let’s use today to narrow this to a workshop-worthy NeuroUnlock extension that feels genuinely new but is still something we can validate in about six weeks. I’d like us to leave with one primary direction and one backup, and both should be framed so a lightweight prototype gives us signal quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as 'lightweight prototype' really means we don't quietly sign up for retracing or touching the profiler path. The assets are strong, but the brittle parts are exactly the collection and curation stack. If we stay on existing traces and mostly the current seq2seq training loop, I can move fast.
turns.utterance: From the original project, the big assets are still in good shape: we have the RTX 2080 Ti trace corpus, the preprocessing pipeline, and the seq2seq codebase for the inversion side. The expensive pieces to change are the profiling path and anything that forces us to redo large chunks of curation, so if we want a lightweight prototype, it would be great to stay close to the benchmark materials we already trust.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll push 'generalization' as the headline, but I mean transfer across held-out obfuscation templates and architecture families within the same established setup. That's enough for a workshop story if we package it well. And 'new obfuscators' can just be additional stochastic ReDLock-style variants we didn't include before.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, generalization is the right headline, but it only lands if it transfers under a materially different execution setting. Otherwise reviewers will call it in-distribution. If we can show it survives a changed environment and the benchmark remains reproducible, that's defensible and worth doing.
turns.utterance: I like the generalization framing. I think it becomes especially compelling if we can say the attack transfers under a newer execution setting and still looks reproducible, because then the story feels less like a one-off fit to the original benchmark.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with the phrase 'keep the collection setup stable'; that's exactly what I want. We can keep everything on the same trace pipeline and probe whether the decoder handles more stochastic obfuscation families. That gives us a novelty hook without rebuilding infrastructure.
turns.utterance: Right, so maybe the first pass is a lightweight prototype where we keep the collection setup stable and ask whether the decoder can cope with new obfuscators that inject more stochasticity. If that works, we immediately have a sharper transfer narrative.

turns.inner_thought: As long as 'keep the collection setup stable' means no hidden new data generation or relabeling burden. I should anchor us on minimal code changes and already curated traces before this grows legs. If we can do the prototype entirely from the existing materials, I can commit.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me as a starting point. I’d just want the lightweight prototype to mean minimal code changes on top of the current training scripts, and ideally no hidden data regeneration work—if we can begin from the traces we’ve already curated, the turnaround will be much better.

turns.inner_thought: I should define success in a way that helps the paper tell a downstream-security story. For me, a usable recovered model is one that is close enough in topology to preserve attack utility, even if some hidden dimensions are estimated rather than exact. That matches the strongest practical message from NeuroUnlock.
turns.utterance: On the evaluation side, I think success should not just be token-level decoding quality. We should ask whether we recover a usable recovered model and whether that still gives us the downstream adversarial gain that people remembered from NeuroUnlock.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but the recovered model needs to really deserve that name. If it preserves architecture details closely enough and remains stable when the traces get noisier, then the result will read as serious architecture recovery rather than just utility chasing. That also ties naturally into the generalization claim I care about.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if the recovered model stays stable under noise while preserving the architecture details well enough, the paper will look much stronger. That would connect the downstream result to the broader generalization story rather than making it feel like a narrow metric win.

turns.inner_thought: Let me narrow this so we don't sprawl. Candidate one: robustness to randomized obfuscation variants. Candidate two: make the decoder learn an obfuscation family rather than a single procedure, still all within our existing ecosystem. Both can be instantiated using fresh combinations from the same family of defenses.
turns.utterance: Let me try to compress the brainstorm into two candidate directions. One is robustness to randomized obfuscation, where we emphasize performance on new obfuscators. The other is a decoder that learns to invert obfuscation families rather than single procedures, which still gives us a generalization angle but with a more modeling-centric story.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with those, but I want to preserve the possibility of testing transfer under a changed profiling regime. To me that is the implementation-side version of the same story: does the inversion model survive when the execution conditions shift? If that's too much for primary scope, it can still shape the backup.

turns.inner_thought: Good enough. I'll lock the primary around generalization on new obfuscators with a recovered model demo, because that is the fastest route to a polished workshop submission. The changed-regime idea can sit as backup unless it turns out to be cheap inside the current setup. I don't need to resolve the exact boundaries right now.
turns.utterance: I think the primary direction should be the generalization story: a lightweight prototype on new obfuscators, plus a recovered model demonstration tied to downstream evaluation.
